Auxetic Tessellation

GeometryAreaPhysics
Game: Four stiff rectangles are hinged at their corners, and copies of the group tile the plane.
How to play: Drag A, B or C with a mouse or finger, or focus a dot and use the arrow keys. Change the sliders and press Stretch to see how the pattern reacts.
Colour
Look for the math

The page calls this a model of an auxetic material: something that gets thicker, not thinner, when you pull it. The applet builds the model from four rectangles and asks what happens when their hinges turn.

Four rectangles on a parallelogram

Drag A, B or C. The fourth corner D is placed so that ABCD is a parallelogram: D = A + C − B. One rectangle hangs off each side. The applet turns a side through a quarter turn to get the second direction, then scales it by the slider value alpha on sides AB and CD and gamma on sides BC and DA. A quarter turn makes the two directions perpendicular, so every tile stays a rectangle, even while the hinge rhombus opens and the tiles swing. Setting the two sliders differently gives rectangles of two shapes, not just rotated copies of one.

Why the copies fit exactly

Write u = B − A and w = C − B. Comparing the corners of neighbouring tiles gives four translation steps; the logic test checks them for every slider pair and thousands of random hinges:

v02 = (v01 + v03) / 2  and  v13 = (v01 − v03) / 2.

Because the half-steps land on tile corners too, translating the group of four by the lattice vectors v01 and v03 fills the plane with no gaps. That is what the Layers control draws: more and more rings of the same tessellation.

What stretching really does

With the hinges locked, the sides AB and BC keep their lengths. Let k = |u × w| be the area of the hinge parallelogram; opening a narrow rhombus makes k grow. The four tiles inside one repeat cover 2(alpha|u|² + gamma|w|²) of a cell whose area is

cell = 2(alpha|u|² + gamma|w|²) + 2k(1 + alpha·gamma).

The covered part cannot change, so as the hinge opens the cell grows and the fraction of it covered falls. That is the page's "lowering density". The logic test checks this for all 22 × 22 slider pairs and 41 hinge angles: the cell grows and the density falls in every single case. With alpha = gamma = 1 the dancing squares also grow in both lattice directions, which is the negative Poisson ratio the article describes.

Where the applet is looser than the story

The live page embeds the applet with Loose=1, so normally you may drag all three corners freely; tick Lock hinges to get the fixed-side model the article talks about. Also, the page says stretching always increases thickness. That is true for squares and for the starting sliders, but at extreme slider pairs one lattice direction eventually turns back while the cell still grows and the density still falls. The logic test finds that counterexample, so this page states the exact claim instead of the blanket one. (The applet also contains a second layer-growing routine that its Compute() never calls; it has no effect on what you see.)

Set both sliders to 1, tick Lock hinges, press Reset and then Stretch a few times: watch the spaces between the squares open in both directions.
